tldr: O-MAPL is an end-to-end preference-based learning framework for cooperative multi-agent RL that directly learns soft Q-functions from offline pairwise trajectory preferences, avoiding the unstable two-phase approach of separate reward modeling and policy optimization.
contributions: Introducing O-MAPL, an algorithm that exploits the one-to-one mapping between reward and soft Q-functions in MaxEnt RL to learn policies directly from preference data without an explicit reward model.

Proposing a linear value factorization method under CTDE with theoretical proofs of convexity (Proposition 4.1) and local-global consistency, and showing two-layer mixing networks break these properties (Proposition 4.2).
Demonstrating through extensive experiments on SMAC and MAMuJoCo benchmarks that O-MAPL consistently outperforms existing methods across various tasks.
methods: The authors formulate multi-agent PbRL in the Q-space by leveraging the inverse soft Bellman operator to map preferences directly onto Q-functions rather than reward functions. Under a CTDE framework, global Q_tot and V_tot are factorized into local functions via a linear mixing network M_w. Training alternates between maximizing the concave preference likelihood loss L(q,v,w) and minimizing the convex extreme-V loss J(v) to approximate the log-sum-exp constraint. Local policies are extracted using a weighted behavior cloning approach that preserves global-local consistency.
results: O-MAPL consistently outperforms existing methods across various tasks on both SMAC and MAMuJoCo benchmarks using preference data generated by rule-based and large language model approaches. Theoretically, the preference-based loss L is proven concave in q and w (Proposition 4.1), and the extreme-V loss J is convex in v, guaranteeing unique convergence. Two-layer mixing networks were shown to break convexity (Proposition 4.2) and cause over-fitting, confirming the superiority of the linear design.
limitations: The convexity and local-global consistency guarantees hold only under single-layer (linear) mixing structures; two-layer networks break both properties. Simple local-value-based policy extraction can produce infeasible policies requiring normalization that disrupts GLC. The approach assumes decomposable behavior policies and may face challenges in environments with continuous action spaces where log-sum-exp computation is impractical without the XQL approximation.
